passage: Note by Zeenat, warehouse supervisor. Friday: the outgoing coordinator handed Lalit the dispatch schedule ten minutes before the bus. Lalit did not just say "okay". Lalit repeated it back: "So from Monday I own the morning dispatch list, the transporter calls and the damage register. The Tuesday truck needs a confirmation call the day before. Have I missed anything?" The coordinator paused. "The gate pass book. Also the transporter changes on the fifteenth." Lalit wrote both down, asked where the gate pass book is kept, and got the spare key. Monday ran smoothly. I intend to have every new owner say what they now own before the giver leaves. - Zeenat

qa.q: What three things did Lalit say would be owned from Monday?
qa.a: Lalit named the morning dispatch list, the transporter calls and the damage register.

qa.q: What did Lalit want to achieve by repeating everything back?
qa.a: Lalit felt responsible and cautious, wanting to be sure of what Lalit now owned and to catch anything missing before the giver left.

qa.q: What would probably have happened without the repeat-back step?
qa.a: The gate pass book and the transporter change on the fifteenth would have been missed, causing confusion later.

qa.q: How might the outgoing coordinator have felt when Lalit asked "Have I missed anything?"
qa.a: Prompted to recall the missing details, and probably relieved to be asked so the handoff was complete.

grounding: Shows a receiver repeating back what they now own and asking for anything missing before the giver leaves.

passage: Wednesday. Vikas leaves for the other office tomorrow, and today he gave me the training schedule for new hires. Instead of nodding and rushing to my meeting, I said, "Let me say what I now own: booking the room every Monday, sending the joining kit, and the feedback form on day five. Anything else?" Vikas laughed. "Yes, laptop requests go through IT by Thursday. I always forgot to tell people that." I would have missed it. I also asked for the shared calendar login, which came within a minute. Then I emailed the three points back to Vikas so we both had them in writing. Felt slightly silly, but much calmer. - Baljeet

passage:
Manjula had run the ration shop register in Karanjgaon for twenty-two years. On her last evening before retiring, she sat with Pradeep, who would take over, on the bench outside the shop.
She talked fast, pages flipping. Pradeep listened. Then he said, "Tai, let me tell it back so you can correct me." He counted on his fingers. "I open Monday and Thursday. I update the register every evening. I give the monthly list to the supply office on the 28th. Right?"
"And the widows' list," Manjula said. "They get their rice first."
"Where is that list?"
She blinked, then pulled out a folded paper from her blouse. "I kept it with me."
"And the spare key? And the two families who haven't collected for two months?"
They went through each one while the sun went down. Pradeep wrote everything in a new notebook. The next month, not a single family came asking where their rice was.

qa.q: On which days does Pradeep open the shop?
qa.a: Monday and Thursday.

qa.q: How did Manjula seem to feel when Pradeep asked where the widows' list was?
qa.a: Manjula looked surprised, realising she had kept it with her and nearly left without handing it over.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that avoided confusion later?
qa.a: Pradeep repeated back what he now owned, asked about every missing item before Manjula left and wrote it all in a notebook.

qa.q: How might the families feel the next month?
qa.a: The families would feel relieved and secure, since nobody had to come asking where their rice was.

grounding: Shows a receiver who repeats back his new duties and asks for missing items before the giver leaves, closing the loop at handover.

passage:
At the community food bank in Leeds, Nkechi was moving to another city on Saturday. Noa would take over the volunteer schedule.
Nkechi handed her a laptop and a ring binder. "It's all in here. You'll be fine."
Noa pulled up a chair. "Can I tell it back to you first? I own the weekly rota, the Friday reminder texts, and finding cover when someone drops out."
"Yes, exactly."
"What about the Wednesday school pick-ups? The binder has a page, but no names."
Nkechi paused. "Oh. Those are Dennis and his daughter. I just ring them. It's not written anywhere."
"And the storeroom key?"
"Behind the kettle."
Noa wrote both on the first page of the binder. Then she read the whole list aloud once more. Nkechi laughed. "I think you know it better than me now."
Three weeks later, Dennis got a call from Noa every Tuesday, just as before.

qa.q: Where is the storeroom key?
qa.a: Behind the kettle.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel when Noa read the list aloud at the end?
qa.a: Nkechi felt amused and reassured, laughing that Noa knew it better now.

qa.q: What did Noa's questions uncover?
qa.a: They uncovered that the Wednesday school pick-ups depended on a phone call to Dennis that was never written down.

qa.q: What would change if Noa had just said, "Thanks, I'll be fine"?
qa.a: The Wednesday pick-ups might have quietly stopped, because Dennis would never have got his call.

grounding: Illustrates a receiver who repeats back what she now owns and asks about gaps before the giver leaves.

passage:
On Afreen's last afternoon at the district health office, she handed Ishita a thick folder. "The vaccination camp registrations are yours now. It's all in there."
Ishita opened it but didn't let her go yet. "Can I say back what I think I own? From Monday I collect the village lists from the health workers, enter them by Thursday, and send the final count to the camp doctor."
"Yes, exactly."
"What's not in the folder? Anything half-done?"
Afreen paused. "Oh. Kharkhoda sent their list on paper, not by email. It's in my drawer, not entered yet. And the doctor prefers a phone call if the count changes after Thursday."
Ishita wrote both on a sticky note and stuck it to the laptop. "Anyone I should call if I get stuck?"
"Suresh in accounts knows the old sheets."
Ishita read all three points back once more. Afreen laughed. "You've just saved me three worried phone calls next week."

qa.q: Where was the Kharkhoda list?
qa.a: It was on paper in Afreen's drawer, not entered yet.

qa.q: What might Afreen have felt when Ishita asked what was not in the folder?
qa.a: Afreen seemed briefly caught off guard, pausing before remembering the paper list, and then relieved, laughing that Ishita had saved three worried phone calls.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's questions did the most good, and why?
qa.a: "What's not in the folder? Anything half-done?" brought out the paper list and the doctor's preference while Afreen was still there to ask.

qa.q: What would change if Ishita had just said "Okay, thanks" and taken the folder?
qa.a: The Kharkhoda list might have sat unentered in the drawer, the count could have been wrong, and next week would have meant confusion and chasing Afreen.

grounding: Shows a receiver repeating back what they now own and asking what is missing before the person handing over leaves.
